segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The farmhouse stood a quarter of a mile back along the road, and its mistress let them the kitchen and their supper for two shillings, having satisfied herself that the gentleman was married to neither of the young women and then, being a practical woman, deciding she did not much care. The driver walked on to Itchen Vale. That left the fire, two settles, and the farmer's wife asleep over her mending within the half hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith took the dispensing book and a candle to the far settle, which was the nearest thing to leaving the room that the kitchen allowed.

segments.speaker: Miss Hester Lamb
segments.text: You have never once said where you were.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: You have never once asked.

segments.speaker: Miss Hester Lamb
segments.text: I am asking now. There is nowhere for either of us to go until morning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It came in the flattest voice she had ever heard used upon such matters.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: My horse went down in a ford I never learnt the name of, and I went down under the horse. They carried me to a house at Lisbon that had been a convent. I was thirteen months in it, and for nine of those I could not have told you what county I was born in.

segments.speaker: Miss Hester Lamb
segments.text: Thirteen months.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: The regiment went up into France without me, and some clerk with a great deal to do drew a line through my name. I do not blame the clerk. I have been that clerk.

segments.speaker: Miss Hester Lamb
segments.text: And you wrote.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: Twice, when I could hold a pen, to my great-uncle. Nothing came back. Anything sent to me went after the regiment, and a letter to a man in a hospital is a letter to nobody in particular.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fire dropped. Hester put her hands together in her lap and looked at them, which for her was very nearly hiding.

segments.speaker: Miss Hester Lamb
segments.text: We had it in the November of the year thirteen. Mrs Pike brought it out to Upper Barton with the rest of the news, and I said how very shocking, and went into the dairy and finished the butter.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: That is what one says.

segments.speaker: Miss Hester Lamb
segments.text: It is. I also took the third volume of Anson out of the library that week and kept it eleven months, and told my father I had mislaid it. It was under my bed. I could not have worn black for you, Captain; the parish would have wanted to know on what grounds. So I kept your book instead, and now you know a thing about me that nobody else does.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not answer that at all, which she found she preferred to any of the things he might have said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From the far settle, where she had been reading the same page for some while, Judith spoke without looking up.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: She wrote in April, and Mr Hartwell had taken charge of the post in March. A letter out of Oakmere goes down the lane to the Bell for the coach, and somebody must carry it. That somebody had been him for six weeks.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: He never saw her write it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: He did not need to. She put it into his hand and told him what it was. She is not a woman who hands over a thing without explaining it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Farr turned that over. The arithmetic was not difficult, and that was rather the worst of it.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: If that letter had found me, I should have been at Oakmere by August, and no clerk from Winchester would have come out with a paper in September.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: One man in England lost everything by that letter arriving. He was holding it.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: Then he burnt it in the parlour grate and I shall never prove a word of it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Perhaps. But a man who burns a letter must first decide to be that sort of man, and Mr Hartwell would very much rather not decide anything so plainly. It is far easier to send it with a direction that will never answer, and let the post do the burning. Only the post does not burn things, Captain. It keeps them. Somewhere there is a shelf with that letter on it, and I mean to ask Mr Cobbold in the morning where.
